scopeNotes: New text needs independent review; earlier hashes do not certify it.
Map endpoints are not historical founding or extinction dates.

The two imported records have northern Plains outlines and alternate spellings also attested together in the Smithsonian catalogue. They share one narrative, not two invented polities. Imported intervals 1492 to 1500 and 1530 to 1783 remain unchanged. No card is attached to every Stoney, Dakota, Lakota, Gros Ventre or Canadian First Nation record. Related peoples and shared reservations do not erase separate identities.

The 1492 to 1640 phase uses the first map snapshot only as the start of a coverage window before the European reports discussed by Miller. It makes no founding claim. Miller places dialectal distinction before the sixteenth century, while the NPS and part of the Fort Belknap page offer a seventeenth-century split and other tribal accounts contest a Sioux-origin account. No precise split, etymology or original homeland is asserted as settled.

Miller’s scholarly synthesis supports family-band organization and broad trade chronology. Archaeological identification of the Mortlach aggregate, sacred ceremonies and outdated census totals are not adopted. The page is an attributed synthesis, not a newly inspected excavation report.

The NPS Fort Union page supports excavated objects, food exchange, cooking technique, post dates and the 1837 smallpox episode. Its causal wording blaming visitors and its population numbers are not adopted. The objects come from a multi-community trading post and cannot individually be assigned to Assiniboine owners. The broader-context object item is not falsely dated to 1492. The 1867 endpoint refers only to the post.

The Fort Belknap history combines institutional information with older reprinted ethnography. Only shared government is cited here; no claims of a simple language, universal buffalo-only diet, last surviving buffalo herd, timeless ceremonies or uniform political consent. Material uses are supported separately by Miller. Montana DNRC’s Reservation Setting section supports the 1888 land reduction, not current water-rights advice or a claim that all communities agreed freely. The two reused sources were checked together with their passages in the Aaniiih card, including titles and notes, to keep each underlying source below 200 words across both cards.

The Catlin object record was read, including its 1832 date and label quoting his 1841 account. The image was not independently inspected. No judgement of women’s appearance, identity of the sitters or universal dress code is repeated. The title does not establish that the two sitters were mother and daughter.

The Nelson-Atkins catalogue identifies the 1989 maker as Assiniboine Sioux but explicitly traces this cradle’s form to Kiowa and Comanche examples. This distinction is retained. The toy label and unusually large listed dimensions are not used to infer actual infant use or size. No excavation or physical inspection took place; protective-amulet practice is not transferred to all Assiniboine households.

Blumberg’s artist interview was read in full. The two linked stories jointly remain within one source budget. They concern a contemporary Assiniboine-Sioux family and a Sioux-style dress, not every Assiniboine family. 2007 is the account date, not the grandfather’s ceremony. No superlative award ranking, current residence or count of all the artist’s works is repeated.

The Nakóda Language Project’s indexed About text was read; direct access failed. The December 2017 initiation and subsequent first-year materials support an approximate 2018 item, not completion of the proposed K-12 curriculum. No audio, app or lesson was claimed as independently tested. Bigby’s separate March 2025 firsthand instructor account supports the specific library story session.

FHQ’s Carry the Kettle profile supports the 1877 adhesion and local attachment to Cypress Hills. It is not used for current litigation, disputed reserve creation, massacre totals or a transfer of every Assiniboine land right. The community’s continued identity is not reduced to its colonial administrative name.

The public cultural-resources page describes its 1995 creation, mission and site categories. These categories do not prove exclusive ethnicity, excavation dates or legal ownership of every managed location. Sensitive site coordinates and restricted ceremonial knowledge are not added.

All content is author-checked and awaits independent historical review. Geometry, additional map coverage and successor relations remain unverified. Modern stories are explicitly dated and appear as later history when an early map year is selected.

proposedOverrides.summary: The Assiniboine are a living Indigenous people with communities in the United States and Canada, including Fort Peck and Carry the Kettle Nakoda Nation.

identityEvidence.assessment: Alternate Assiniboine/Assiniboin spellings used for northern Plains outlines and attested by the Smithsonian catalogue’s title and description. Shared people-level narrative; neither outline is a verified village distribution, exclusive sovereignty or founding/extinction chronology.
